claims.text: The initial material is a W–Cu composite with tungsten particles embedded in a copper matrix and non-engineered interfaces.
A controlled boron-diffusion treatment will promote in situ formation of an ultra-thin WC layer at W–Cu interfaces.
An ultra-thin WC interphase will enhance bonding at the W–Cu interface.
An ultra-thin WC interphase will improve phonon coupling across the W–Cu interface.
Improved phonon coupling from the WC interphase will reduce thermal boundary resistance.
Reducing W–Cu thermal boundary resistance will increase the composite's overall thermal conductivity.
The engineered interphase can preserve the composite's mechanical integrity.
The boron-diffusion treatment and resulting WC interphase will not compromise irradiation resistance.
The treated composite will have a statistically significant increase in thermal conductivity relative to an untreated W–Cu composite.
The treated composite will retain mechanical durability comparable to that of the untreated W–Cu composite.
The treated composite will retain irradiation resistance comparable to that of the untreated W–Cu composite.
A standard untreated W–Cu composite has relatively high interfacial thermal resistance that limits heat dissipation.
The predicted benefits will persist during high-temperature cycling and irradiation typical of fusion-reactor joints.
Interphase formation and performance may depend on boron concentration, diffusion time, and treatment temperature.
An optimum WC interphase thickness is needed to balance thermal-conductivity improvement against mechanical performance.

contradictions.description: The stated initial W–Cu system and boron-diffusion treatment provide no identified carbon source, yet the proposed mediator is tungsten carbide (WC). Boron addition would not by itself supply the carbon required to form WC.
